content.text:
All eleven tests pass across the four test files.

Changes, all in `netgraph/graph.py`:
- **is_bipartite** runs a breadth-first 2-colouring from every uncoloured node and returns False on the first edge whose endpoints share a colour. A self-loop fails immediately, since it forms an odd cycle of length one.
- **subgraph** builds a mapping from the given ids to their positions, creates a fresh Graph of that size, and copies each induced edge once. Duplicate ids in the input raise ValueError, and out-of-range ids raise IndexError as elsewhere.
- **common_neighbors** intersects the two adjacency sets and sorts the result.

```
python -m pytest -q
11 passed in 0.03s
```

I also checked self-loops in both new methods and the duplicate-id path of subgraph. All behaved as intended.

**Representation:** the codebase uses Approach A, adjacency lists, implemented as one Python set of neighbours per node. This has not changed at any point in the project. I chose it at the start because every operation in the interface is neighbour-oriented, and none of the later features gave a reason to switch. The matrix idea you raised for remove_node would cost the same O(nodes + edges) for relabelling as the set version does, while adding n² memory. The last three features are also natural on sets: 2-colouring iterates neighbours, subgraph copies induced edges by looking up each neighbour, and common_neighbors is a set intersection.
